in_context.text: Paul has just urged that prayers and thanks be offered for all people, including kings and everyone in authority (2:1-2). This verse gives the reason: such prayer is good and pleasing to God. The next verse explains why, because God wants all people to be saved (2:4).

speaker.text: Paul the apostle, who names himself at the start of the letter. Many critical scholars think a follower wrote in his name, while others defend Paul's authorship.

audience.text: Timothy, Paul's younger co-worker, whom Paul left to lead the church at Ephesus. Through him the instruction reaches that church.

affected.text: The people being prayed for: all people, and in particular kings and all who hold authority.

what.text: The verse states that praying for everyone, rulers included, is good and acceptable before God. It calls God 'our Saviour,' a title the letter also uses in its opening line.

events.text: Paul had left Timothy in Ephesus and gone on to Macedonia. Nero was emperor, and the church was facing false teaching from within.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 62-64, between Paul's first and second Roman imprisonments. Scholarly view: many critical scholars date it around AD 80-110, though others hold to the earlier date.

where.text: The letter was sent to Ephesus, a wealthy port city and capital of the Roman province of Asia, known for its temple of Artemis. The place of writing is not stated; it may have been Macedonia.

purpose.text: Paul gives a reason for his call to pray for all people. He grounds it in what pleases God, not just in the church's wish for a quiet life.

big_picture.text: This is part of a section on prayer and conduct in worship. It leads into a central theme of the letter: God desires all people to be saved, and Christ gave himself a ransom for all.

for_readers.text: Prayer for others, even for rulers, is presented as something God values. Other passages also speak of good deeds as pleasing or acceptable to God.

why_it_matters.text: 'This' points back to what came before. So what God calls good here is the prayer for all people and rulers in verses 1-2, not some new idea.
The word means acceptable or pleasing. In the New Testament it appears only here and in 5:4, so it marks prayer for others as something God welcomes.
The phrase means 'before' or 'in the presence of.' Said of God, it carries the sense of God as witness or judge. The standard is God's view, not human approval.
'Saviour' was often used as a title for kings in the Ptolemaic and Roman periods. Here, right after a call to pray for kings, it is given to God.

takeaway.text: Praying for all people, including those in power, is good and pleasing to God our Saviour, who wants all people to be saved.
